# I.

It is a truly distressing sight, when one wishes to contemplate man, to see him at once tormented by the desire to know, perceiving the reasons for nothing, and yet having the audacity and the temerity to wish to provide reasons for everything. Instead of considering the **darkness** <term>ténèbres: A common metaphor in mystical literature for the state of spiritual ignorance or the "fallen" condition of the human mind.</term> that surrounds him, and beginning by sounding its depth, he advances, not only as if he were sure to dissipate it, but even as if there were no obstacles between *Science* and himself. Soon, even striving to create a *Truth*, he dares to put it in the place of that which he should respect in silence, and over which today he has almost no other right than to desire it and to wait for it.

If so many questions about **Liberty** have been debated in vain, and if they have so often ended in the vague conclusion that man is not even capable of possessing it, it is because we have failed to observe how this human faculty depends on and relates to the **Will**. We have failed to see that this will is the only agent capable of either preserving or destroying liberty; in other words, we search for a stable, unchanging faculty in liberty—one that would manifest within us universally and incessantly, always in the same way, unable to grow or diminish, and always remaining at our command regardless of how we have used it. But how can we conceive of a faculty that belongs to man yet remains independent of his will, when that very will constitutes his fundamental essence? # Of Liberty and of the Will.

Another error, which has led these **observers** <note>The author refers to Enlightenment materialist philosophers who viewed human behavior as purely mechanical.</note> to dismiss the concept of liberty, is that they sought to prove its existence through the very action that proceeds from it; in such a way that, to satisfy them, a single act would have to be able to both be and not be at the same time. Since this is evidently impossible, they concluded that everything that happens must necessarily have happened, and consequently, that there was no liberty at all.

But they should have noticed that the act, and the will which conceived it, can only be consistent and not opposed; that a power which has produced its act cannot then stop its effect; and finally, that liberty—even taken in its common sense <term>vulgar sense: the everyday, non-philosophical understanding of a word</term>—does not consist in being able to do the "for" and the "against" <note>original: "le pour & le contre"</note> at the same time, but in being able to do one and the other alternately. Now, even if it were only in this sense, man would sufficiently prove what is commonly called his liberty; since he visibly acts for and against in his various successive actions, and since he is the only being in nature who can avoid always walking the same path.

But it would be to wander strangely astray not to conceive of another idea of liberty; for while this contradiction in a being’s actions proves, it is true, that there is disorder and confusion within his faculties, yet...

### Original State of Man.

->C 2<-

### System of Sensations.

...seek counsel within himself; for, after all, it would be impossible for him to deny the contradiction he would perceive between these two paths. To tell him that he has no laws other than those of his senses, and that he can have no other guide, is to tell him that it would be futile to try to make a choice among the things the senses present to him. Since the senses themselves are subject to variation in their actions, man—unable to control their underlying triggers—would struggle in vain to direct their course and their effects.

But, like a traveler, man cannot deny his own conviction; he clearly sees that the senses bring everything to him. Yet, at the same time, he is forced to admit that among the things they bring, there are some he feels to be good, just as there are others he feels to be bad.

What, then, should be his distrust toward those who would turn him away from making a choice, by insinuating that all these things are indifferent or of the same nature? Should he not—

# Dangers of this System.

—should he not feel the most intense indignation, and be on his guard against such dangerous teachers?

This is, however, I repeat, the most common attempt made against human thought; it is at once the most seductive and the one from which the principle of evil <note>The author likely refers to a spiritual or metaphysical personification of disorder or malice.</note> would draw the greatest advantage. For if it could nurture man in the persuasion that there is no choice to be made among the things surrounding him, it would easily succeed in conveying to him the horrific uncertainty and disorder into which it is itself plunged by its lack of any Law.

But if **Justice** always watches over man, he must possess within himself the means to unravel the stratagems of his enemy and to thwart, whenever he wishes, all its undertakings; otherwise, he could not be punished for allowing himself to be caught by surprise. These means must be founded upon his own nature, which can no more change than the very nature of the **Principle** <term>Principle (*Principe*): In 18th-century mystical and esoteric philosophy, this refers to the divine source or God from which all beings originate.</term> from which he originated. Thus, his own essence, being incompatible with falsehood, makes him realize sooner or later that he is being deceived, and leads him naturally back to **Truth**.

I will therefore employ these very means, which I share with all men, to show them the danger and absurdity of this opinion.

# Universal Quaternary Progression.

This difficulty arises because the difference in the types of all corporeal beings is always in a **Quaternary geometric proportion**. <term>Quaternary geometric proportion: A philosophical concept—central to 18th-century Christian Theosophy—suggesting that nature unfolds according to the number four, and that life forces diminish in a predictable mathematical ratio as they move away from their source.</term> Now, in the true order of things, the higher the degree of the **powers** <note>original: "puissances." Thus, the first terms of the progression, being closer to the **radical term** <term>radical term: The root or originating point of a series, representing the purest form of the life-force before it is divided or weakened by the material world.</term>, have more active properties, which consequently result in more sensible effects, and are thereby easier to distinguish. As this force within the faculties diminishes as the terms of the progression multiply, it is clear that the results of the final terms must possess only nuances that are, in a sense, imperceptible.

This is why the mineral is more difficult to distinguish from the vegetable than the vegetable from the animal; for it is in the mineral that the final term of the progression of created things is found.

# Superiority of Man.

...[I] wanted to show to those who debase him, by confusing him with the **beasts**, that they fall into an unpardonable error concerning him—one that would be inexcusable even regarding purely elementary beings. For from one **kingdom** <note>The "kingdoms" refer to the traditional divisions of nature: mineral, vegetable, and animal.</note> to another, we find infinite differences, even though all these kingdoms share fundamental parities and similarities.

We see that in every class, the lower contains nothing of that which manifests in a particular way in the higher. # Rights of Man over His Thought.

<meta>catchword: All</meta>

The active and intelligent Principle <term>Active Principle</term> <note>In theosophical philosophy, this refers to the soul or the spiritual spark that animates the human being, distinguishing them from purely material or animal existence.</note> which distinguishes him so perfectly from other beings—this Principle must have its own faculties within itself; now, the only one whose use remains to us in our painful situation is that **innate will** within us, which man enjoyed during his **glory** <note>Refers to the "pre-lapsarian" state, or the condition of humanity before the "Fall" from a divine or perfect state.</note> and which he still enjoys after his **fall**. As it is through this will that he went astray, it is by the force of this will alone that he can hope to be restored to his first rights; it is this which preserves him absolutely from the precipices into which some wish to plunge him, and from believing in that **nothingness** <note>A critique of nihilism or strict materialism, which argues that there is no spiritual reality and that death is the end of existence.</note> to which some would wish to reduce his nature: it is through this will, in a word, that while not being the master to prevent good and evil from communicating themselves to him, he is nonetheless responsible for the use he makes of this will, in relation to both. He cannot prevent things from being offered to him, but he can choose, and choose well; and I will give no other proof of this for the moment, except that he suffers, and that he is punished when he chooses poorly.

The intelligent Reader, for whom I write, cannot be unaware that the pain and sufferings of which I wish to speak are of a nature very different from the passing, corporeal, or conventional evils, which are the only ones known to the multitude.

# Seat of the Corporeal Soul.

It is also here that we will learn what we ought to think about a question that commonly concerns men: namely, in which part of the body the **Active Principle** <note>original: "Principe actif" — in this context, the animating force or spiritual essence that gives life to a physical form.</note>, or the soul, is located, and what is the place designated to be the seat of all its operations.

In corporeal and **sensible** <note>Relating to the physical senses or the material world.</note> beings, the **Active Principle** is in the blood, which, like fire, is the source of corporeal life; thus, based on what has been said regarding the different faculties of beings, we cannot deny that its primary seat is in the heart, from which it extends its action to every part of the body.

Let us no longer be hindered by the difficulty raised by those who claimed that if the corporeal soul were in the blood, it would be divided and partially escape when the animal lost blood; for the soul only weakens its action through this loss, in that it loses the means to exercise it. However, the soul itself suffers no alteration, because being simple, it is necessarily **indivisible**.

What we call the **death of bodies** is, therefore, nothing other than the total cessation of this action when it is deprived of its secondary vehicles—as in cases of exhaustion; or when it is too constrained, as in diseases of the **humors** <note>Refers to the pre-modern medical theory that health was governed by the balance of four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>; or finally when it is too free, and thereby intercepted—

Although I declare that life, or the **corporeal soul**, resides in the blood, I must nevertheless remark in passing that the blood is **insensible** <note>Incapable of feeling or perception on its own.</note>; an observation which may make known to men the difference that exists between the faculties of matter and the faculties of the **Principle of matter** <note>The underlying spiritual or formative force that governs physical substance.</note>, and which will prevent them from confounding two such distinct beings.

It is far more evident that, as an **immaterial being**, it is only with an immaterial being that it can have a connection and affinity, and one conceives that with any other being, communication would be impracticable.

### Connection of the Intellectual to the Sensible.

Thus, it is upon the **immaterial corporeal Principle** <note>original: "Principe immatériel corporel" — Referring to the "animal soul" or vital life force that animates the physical body but is not itself material.</note> of man, and not upon any portion of his matter, that his **intellectual Principle** <note>The higher human mind or spirit, distinct from biological life.</note> rests: it is there that it is bound for a time by the higher hand <note>Likely a reference to God or the Divine Architect, suggesting the soul's presence in the body is a form of temporary exile or "condemnation."</note> that has condemned it to it; but by its nature, it dominates the corporeal Principle, just as the corporeal Principle dominates the body; and we should no longer doubt this, in that it is in the upper part, or in the head, where we have previously shown that it manifested all its faculties; in a word, it uses this Principle for the sensible <note>Meaning "perceptible to the senses" or physical.</note> execution of these same faculties; and such is the means of clearly discerning the seat and the use of the two different Principles of man.

->## Tribute Imposed on Man.<-

[It is for] men to acknowledge a **Superior Being** <note>original: "Etre supérieur" — the author’s term for God or the Divine Source.</note>, and to feel that, being attached to a **sensible religion** <note>original: "religion sensible" — a system of faith and ritual that makes use of the physical senses, which the author argues is necessary for humans in their current material state.</note>, there must be a sensible means of conveying their homage to him; it is certain that, despite all their wanderings, the **Law** <note>Referring to the immutable spiritual and natural order of the universe.</note> can never vary for them. ->Uncertainty of Political Thinkers.<-

### 5.

When considering man in his political relations, he will present two points of view, just as in the previous observations: the first, that of what he *could* and *ought* to be in the state of society; the second, that of what he actually *is* in that same state. Now, it is by carefully studying what he ought to be in the state of society that we will learn to better judge what he is today. This comparison is, without a doubt, the only way to clearly reveal the mysteries that still shroud the origin of societies, to establish the rights of **Sovereigns**, and to lay down the rules of **administration** by which **Empires** could and should support and govern themselves.

The greatest difficulty experienced by the **Political Thinkers** <note>original: "Politiques." In the 18th century, this referred to political philosophers or theorists rather than modern elected officials.</note> who have best sought to follow the path of **Nature**, has been to reconcile all social **Institutions** with the principles of justice and equality that they perceive within themselves. As soon as it was shown to them that man was free, they believed him made for independence; and from that point, they judged that all **subjugation** <term>subjugation</term> <note>original: "assujettissement." This refers to the state of being subject to a government, law, or monarch, which Enlightenment thinkers often debated in relation to natural liberty.</note> was contrary to his true essence.

-># On the Sociability of Man.<-

This, let us not doubt, is the true source of society among men, and at the same time the picture where man can learn what is the first of his duties when he becomes a Father.

### On the Sociability of Man.

Why do we find nothing similar among the beasts? It is because they are not of a nature to know such needs; it is because the beast, being directed only by the <term>sensory<note>The original French uses "le sensible," referring to knowledge gained strictly through the physical senses rather than through intellect or moral reasoning.</note></term>, knows nothing once this physical need no longer speaks to it. Because bodily affection is the measure of all its faculties, once this affection is satisfied, there is no more sensibility or desire for it; thus, for the beast, there is no social bond.

One should not cite the example of the attachment of some animals, whether to each other or to man; we are speaking here only of the natural course and movements of beings. Any examples that might be raised against us would surely be the result of habit, which, as we have said elsewhere, can be found in the beast in its capacity as a sentient being.

Nor should one cite those colonies of certain animals that live and travel together, whether on land, in water, or in the air; it is only a specific and sensory need that brings them together. There is so little true attachment among them that one may perish and disappear without the others even noticing.

We see already, then, from these observations on the earliest stages of our material existence, that man is not born to live in isolation.

### On the Sociability of Man.

We see that after his bodily dependence has ceased, there remains for him a link infinitely stronger, in that it relates to his own being; we see, I say, that through an interest inseparable from his current state, he will always seek out his fellows, and that if they never deceived him, or if he were not already corrupted, he would not think at all of distancing himself from them, even when his body no longer needed their help.

### Of the Dignity of Kings.

...increase, yet contains nothing that is not consistent with the idea we find ourselves holding regarding Kings, when we wish to examine it more deeply.

Reflecting upon the respect we bear them, do we not see that we regard them as being the image and representatives of a higher hand <note>original: "main supérieure"; a common Enlightenment-era euphemism for God or Divine Providence</note>, and as such, capable of more virtue, strength, light, and wisdom than other men? Is it not with a kind of regret that we see them exposed to human weaknesses? And do we not seem to desire that they make themselves known only through acts as great and sublime as the hand that is believed to have placed them all upon the **Throne**?

Indeed, is it not under this sacred authority that they present themselves and assert all their rights? Though we may not have the certainty that they act through it, is it not from our feeling the possibility of it that there arises that kind of awe <note>original: "effroi"; in this context, it implies a respectful dread or religious awe rather than simple terror</note> resulting from their power, and that veneration they inspire in us?

All this indicates to us, then, that their primary origin is superior to the powers and will of men, and should confirm us in the idea I have presented: that their source is above those which <term>Political Science</term> <note>original: "la Politique"; referring to the secular study of governance and social contracts</note> has sought for them.

## Of the Science of Kings.

As for these faculties and these innumerable *virtues* that we have shown to be present in Kings who have recovered their ancient light <note>The "ancient light" refers to a state of original spiritual wisdom or divine enlightenment that the author believes monarchs should ideally possess.</note>, it is still the Leaders of established Societies who herald them to us, since they act as if they possessed the enjoyment of everything we feel ought to be within them.

# On Legitimate *Governments*.

I would not be believed, no doubt, if I wished to persuade anyone that all established *Governments* are conformed to the model we have just seen, because in effect the greatest number of them are very far from it; but I beg my fellow men to be fully convinced that true *Sovereigns*, as well as legitimate *Governments*, are not imaginary beings; that there have been such at all times, that there are such currently, and that there will always be such, because this enters into the Universal Order, and because, finally, this pertains to the *Great Work* <note>The "Great Work" (*Grand Œuvre*) in this philosophical context refers to the spiritual evolution and perfection of humanity, rather than just the alchemical pursuit of turning lead into gold.</note>, which is something other than the *Philosopher’s Stone*.

A third difficulty, which will naturally arise from the principles that have been established, is having seen therein that every man, by his nature, may hope to recover the light he has lost, and yet that I recognize *Sovereigns* among men; for, if every man reaches the term of his restoration <note>original: "réhabilitation." In this school of thought, this refers to the process of man returning to his original, divine state before the Fall.</note>, who will be the leaders? Will all men not be equal? Will they not all be Kings?

This difficulty can no longer persist after what I have said regarding the obstacles that so often halt man in his path <note>original: "carrière," meaning one's course of life or spiritual progress.</note>, and which—further multiplied by his imprudences and the false use of his will—are, on his part, so rarely and so unequally overcome.

# On the Military Institution.

<page-num>291</page-num>

We could even recall here what I have said concerning the natural differences in the intellectual faculties of men, where it could be observed that, even when comparing them only from this point of view, there would always remain an inequality between them; yet it is an inequality that would not be at all painful to them, and which would not humiliate them; because their greatness would be real within each of them, and not relative, like that which is merely conventional and arbitrary.

# On the Inequality of Men.

...men will all reach that degree of greatness and perfection which would make them independent of one another; thus, as long as this state of <term>reprobation</term> <note>original: "réprobation"; in this philosophical context, it refers to a state of being "cast out" or the fallen condition of humanity</note> persists, if they have always had leaders chosen from among themselves, it must be expected that they will always have them; this is even indispensable until this time of punishment is entirely fulfilled.

It is therefore with confidence that I base the origin of a man's authority over his fellow men, that of power, and all the titles of **political sovereignty**, upon his <term>rehabilitation</term> <note>original: "réhabilitation"; the process of a human being being restored to their original spiritual dignity or status</note> within his <term>Principle</term> <note>original: "Principe"; a term frequently used in 18th-century mystical philosophy to refer to God or the Divine Source</note>.

I do not even fear to assert that this is the sole and unique way to explain all rights, and to reconcile the multitude of differing opinions that <term>political theorists</term> <note>original: "Politiques"; referring to authors and philosophers who write on the nature of the state and law</note> have brought forth on this matter; for, to recognize a superiority in one being over others of the same class, one must not seek it in those ways in which he resembles them, but rather in those ways in which he can be distinguished from them.

Now, by their current nature, men being condemned to <term>deprivation</term> <note>original: "privation"; the state of spiritual lack or being "deprived" of the full presence of the Divine</note>, they all resemble one another absolutely in this regard, with only slight nuances; it is therefore only by striving to make this deprivation disappear that they can hope to establish real differences between one another.

# On Adultery

...adultery was the cause of the deprivation and the ignorance in which man is still plunged, and that it is this which changed his state of light and splendor into a state of darkness and <term>ignominy<gloss>deep personal humiliation or disgrace</gloss></term>. <note>The author is likely referring to the "Primal Adultery"—a common theme in Martinist philosophy where the first man "prostituted" his spiritual powers to the material realm.</note>

It is also in this corporal adultery that man could easily form an idea of the evils he prepares for the <term>fruits of his crimes<gloss>children born from these unions</gloss></term>, by reflecting that this universal temporal cause, or this superior will, does not preside over <term>assemblages<gloss>unions or procreative acts</gloss></term> that it has not approved, and even less so over those it condemns; that if its presence is necessary to everything that exists temporally, whether sensible or intellectual, man strips his <term>offspring<gloss>original: "postérité"</gloss></term> of this support when he begets them according to an illegitimate will; and that consequently, he exposes this offspring to unheard-of <term>sufferings<gloss>original: "pâtimens"—an archaic term for spiritual or physical afflictions</gloss></term>, and to the terrible decay of all the faculties of their being.

### 332

->**On the Right of Life and Death.**<-

But, just as no man in his current state can have a just **authority** over his fellow beings without having, through his own efforts, recovered the faculties he has lost, so too, whatever this **authority** may be, it cannot reveal in him the right to bodily punish his fellow beings, nor the **right of life and death** over men; since he did not possess this right of physical life and death even during his time of glory, over the **Subjects** submitted to his **Domination**.

For that to be the case, his empire would have had to expand through his fall, and he would have had to acquire new **Subjects**. But, far from having increased their number, we see on the contrary that he has lost the **authority** he held over the original ones; we even see that the only kind of superiority he can acquire over his fellow beings is that of correcting them when they go astray; of *stopping* them when they give themselves over to *crime*, or rather, that of supporting them by bringing them closer—through his example and his **virtues**—to the state they no longer enjoy; and not the power to exercise over them, by his own accord, a rule that their very nature disavows.

# On Extension.
<meta>catchword: will</meta>

To make this even more palpable, it is appropriate to fix our ideas on the nature of **extension**<term>the quality of occupying space; the primary property of matter in Cartesian and occult philosophy</term>. Extension is, like all other properties of bodies, a production of the **Generating Principle** of matter, according to the **Laws** and the order which are prescribed to this inferior Principle by the **superior Principle** that directs it. In this sense, extension, being nothing more than a **secondary production**, cannot have the same advantages as those beings included in the class of **primary productions**; the latter possess their fixed Laws within themselves; all their properties are invariable because they are united with their essence. It is there, in a word, where **weight, number, and measure**<note>A reference to Wisdom of Solomon 11:20: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight," a foundational concept in Western alchemy and Christian Neoplatonism.</note> are so regulated that they can no more be altered than the being itself can be destroyed.

If this is so, the extension of bodies is therefore no more determined for us with certainty than their other properties. When, therefore, to make the value of this extension known to us, one makes use of a **measure** taken from within this same extension, this measure that is employed...

# The Nature of the Circumference.

This is the source of the predicament that **Geometers** <term>historically, this refers to mathematicians and natural philosophers who studied the laws of physical space</term> experience when they wish to measure curves; for the measurement they use, having been designed for the straight line, is only suited to that type of line, and presents insurmountable difficulties when one wishes to apply it to the circular line, as well as to any other curve derived from it.

I say that this measurement then presents insurmountable difficulties; for, although Geometers have *cut the knot* <note>The author uses the phrase "tranché le nœud," a reference to the Gordian Knot, implying they have bypassed a complex problem with a bold but flawed simplification.</note> by presenting the circular line to us as an assembly of **infinitely small** straight lines, they would be wrong to believe they had resolved the question in this way, since a falsehood has never been able to resolve anything.

Now, I cannot help but regard this definition as false, since it directly contradicts the idea that they themselves and Nature give us of a **circumference**, which is nothing other than a line where all points are equally distant from a common center; and I do not even know how Geometers can reasonably rely on two such contradictory propositions; for, after all, if the circumference is merely an assembly of straight lines, however **infinitely small** one supposes them to be, all the points of this circumference will never be equally distant from the center, because

Is it not, as a perpendicular <note>The "perpendicular" here represents a moral and physical uprightness that provides the "base and foundation" for all existence.</note>, to regulate the base and the foundation of all beings, and to trace for each of them their Laws?

On the contrary, does not the circular line limit, at all its points, the productions of the straight line? Consequently, does it not continually tend to destroy it, and can it not be regarded in some way as its enemy? So, how would it then be possible that two things so opposite in their course, and which have such different properties, would not be distinguished in their *number*, just as they are in their *action*?

# Of the Straight Line

### Of the Earth.

...things <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "the most precious thing..."</note> should evaluate His works, and that their value lay not rather in the nobility of their purpose and in their properties, than in the grandeur of the space and the extent that they occupy.

But he did not fear the indolence and cowardice that necessarily follow from this feigned modesty; and if man avoids seeing himself today as meant to be the King of the Universe, it is because he lacks the courage to work toward recovering its *Titles*, because the duties thereof seem too tiring to him, and because he fears less to renounce his state and all his rights than to undertake restoring them to their full value. However, if he wished for a moment to observe himself, he would soon see that he ought to place his humility in admitting that he is rightly below his rank, but not in believing himself to be of a nature that could never have occupied it, nor could ever return to it.

### On the Number Nine.

No doubt it will offend no one to consider a circumference as a **zero**; for what figure can resemble a circumference more than a zero? I am not speaking of the order in which these three signs should be arranged to conform with the order of the faculties they represent; this order has undoubtedly been inverted by passing through human hands, and almost all the languages of nations vary on this point. But since the true language is unique <note>This refers to the philosophical concept of a "Universal" or "Original" language, often associated with the biblical idea of the language spoken by Adam, which was believed to perfectly express the nature of reality before being lost or corrupted.</note>, the arrangement of these signs would not have been subject to all these contrasts, had man known how to preserve it.

One must not believe, however, that even in the true language <note>The author refers to a theoretical "original" or "universal" language where words perfectly match the essence of the things they describe.</note>, these three signs were always arranged in the same order as they are within our intellectual faculties; for these signs are merely their sensible expression <note>The physical manifestation of thought, such as spoken sound or written symbols.</note>, and I have agreed that the sensible could never follow the same path as the intellectual. Furthermore, as we have already seen, this language would have had the advantage of being shielded from all ambiguity and of always possessing the same meaning, because it is bound to the nature of things, and the nature of things is invariable.

Among the three fundamental signs to which every expression of our thoughts is subject, there is one that deserves our attention above the others, and upon which we shall cast our eyes for a moment; it is the one that links the other two, which is the image of action among our intellectual faculties, and the image of <term>Mercury</term> <note>In the philosophical and alchemical traditions of the author's time, Mercury represents the fluid, mediating principle that connects opposites or links the spiritual to the material.</note> among corporeal principles; in a word, it is that which is called the *Verb* among Grammarians.

One must not forget, therefore, that if it is the image of action, it is upon it that the entire **sensible work** <note>The "sensible work" refers to the physical world and the external manifestation of thoughts through speech and action.</note> is supported; and that since the property of action is to do everything, that of its sign or its image is to represent and indicate everything that is being done.

Also, let us reflect on the properties of this sign in the composition of speech; let us see that the more it is strong and expressive, the more the results arising from it are perceptible and distinct; let us follow this easy-to-conduct experiment: that even in all things subject to human power or conventions, the effect is regulated, determined, and animated primarily by the verb. Finally, let the **Observers** <note>The author frequently uses "Observers" to describe those who study the spiritual and hidden laws of nature rather than just surface appearances.</note> examine whether it is not through this sign called the *Verb*, that everything we know as most intellectual and most active within us is manifested; whether it is not the only one of the three signs <note>The three signs of the author's linguistic theory: the Agent (Noun), the Action (Verb), and the Subject or Product.</note> capable of strengthening or weakening the expression, while the names of the agent and the subject, once fixed, always remain the same. It is by this that we shall judge if we were justified in attributing action to it, since it is truly the repository of it, and its help is absolutely necessary for anything to be done, or even tacitly expressed.

It is here that we should observe why idle Observers and speculative <term>Caballists</term> <note>Derived from Kabbalah, referring here to those who study the mystical or hidden meanings of letters and words, often in a purely theoretical or "speculative" manner.</note>—

On the contrary, since these faculties are themselves different from one another, and since we can observe striking distinctions therein, it is natural to think that their fruits must indicate this difference, and that they cannot resemble one another; but at the same time, as these faculties are essentially linked, and as it is entirely impossible for one to act without the help of the others, we see thereby that it is necessary for the same connection to reign between their different kinds of productions, and that they all proclaim the same origin.

# On the Characters of Writing

characters of the **true language** <note>original: "langue vraie." The author refers to a primordial or divine system of communication where symbols are not arbitrary but directly reflect the essence of the things they represent.</note>, and their enormous variety which introduced such a great diversity into human languages, that few of them use the same signs, and even those that agree on this point still vary in their quantity, by admitting or rejecting some signs, each according to its particular idiom and its unique spirit.

But, just as the characters of the **true language** are as numerous as the beings contained within **Nature**, so it is equally certain that none of these characters can take its origin except from this same **Nature**; and it is from her that they draw everything that serves to distinguish them, since outside of her, there is nothing perceptible. This is also why, despite the variety of characters that human languages employ, they can never go beyond these same boundaries, and it is always from lines and from figures that they are obliged to take all the signs of their <term>convention</term> <note>socially agreed-upon symbols, as opposed to "natural" signs</note>; this proves in an evident manner that men can invent nothing.

We will be convinced of all this by some observations on the art of **Painting**, which we can look upon as having taken its birth from the characters of the language in question, just as human **Poetry** had taken its birth from its verbal expression.

# On Painting.

->Ii 2<-
<meta>catchword: But</meta>

If it is certain that this language is unique, and as ancient as time itself, one cannot doubt that the **characters** <note>original: "caractères." In this mystical context, these are not just letters, but the inherent symbolic forms or "signatures" that define every being in nature.</note> it employs were the first **models**. Those men who applied themselves to studying it often needed to aid their memory with notes and copies. Now, it was in these copies that the greatest precision was required; for within this multitude of characters—which are sometimes distinguished only by the slightest difference—it is certain that the smallest alteration could distort and confuse them.

One must sense that if men had been wise, they would have made no other use of **Painting**; indeed, for the very sake of this **Art**, they would have been fortunate to restrict themselves to the imitation and copying of these primary characters. For if they are, with good reason, so discerning about the choice of models, where could they have found any truer or more regular than those which expressed the very nature of things? If they are so fastidious regarding the quality and use of **colors**, where could they have better applied themselves than to forms that each carried their own proper color? Finally, if they desire lasting paintings, how could they have succeeded better than by copying them from objects that are forever new, and with which they can at any moment compare their own productions?

# On Intellectual Measure

Such is therefore the inferiority of <term>artificial music</term> <note>original: "Musique artificielle"; refers to music composed and performed by humans, contrasting it with the "natural" or "divine" harmony of the universe.</note> and of all <term>sensible things</term>, <note>Physical objects or phenomena that can be perceived through the five senses.</note> that they contain only passive actions, and that their measure, though determined in itself, can only be known to us in relation to other measures with which we compare them.

Among things of a higher order and absolutely beyond the realm of the sensible, this measure reveals itself with more noble features: there, each being, having its own individual action, also possesses within its <term>Laws</term> <note>original: "Loix"; in this context, the metaphysical principles or spiritual rules governing a being’s existence.</note> a measure proportioned to that action. But at the same time, as each of these actions is always new, and always different from the one that precedes it and the one that follows it, it is easy to see that the measure accompanying them can never be the same; thus, it is not in this class of beings that one must seek that uniformity of measure which reigns in Music and in sensible things.

In perishable nature, everything exists in a state of dependence, and displays only a blind execution, which is nothing other than the forced assembly of several agents subject to the same law; these agents, always concurring toward the same goal and in the same manner, can only produce a uniform result, provided they encounter no disruption or obstacles to the fulfillment of their action.

# Rights of the True Language.

...all his fellow beings as the essence that constitutes them and establishes a universal resemblance between them.

# Conclusion.

If they have so little reason to congratulate themselves on their successes, it is no longer to the weakness of their nature, nor to the limits of their faculties, that they must attribute it, but solely to the false path they take to reach the goal. This is because they do not observe with sufficient attention that every class of being has its own measure and its own **Law**. It belongs to the **senses** to judge of **sensible things** <term>choses sensibles: physical objects or phenomena that can be perceived by the five senses.</term>, because as long as these are not felt by the body, they achieve nothing; but it belongs to the **intelligence** to judge of **intellectual things** <term>choses intellectuelles: non-material realities, such as ideas, spirits, or divine truths, which belong to the realm of the mind.</term>, of which the senses can know nothing. To wish thus to apply the Laws and measure of one class to the other is evidently to go beyond the order dictated by the very nature of things, and consequently to stray from the only means there was to discern their truth.

I have therefore believed that I was offering my fellow men only truths that are easy to perceive, by telling them that what they seek is only in the **center**. ...than they have; to this admission, I will add that it would be impossible for me to deceive myself on this point, for I have the proof that I know nothing.

This is why I have so often announced that I do not pretend to lead them to the final goal; it is enough for me to have somehow forced them to agree that the blind path of the **human sciences** <note>The secular, materialist academic disciplines of the Enlightenment which the author views as disconnected from spiritual reality.</note> brings them even less close to the goal they seek, since it leads them even to doubt that such a goal exists.

By this, I compel them to admit that by stripping the sciences of the only **Principle** <note>original: "Principe"; for Saint-Martin, this refers to the divine or spiritual source that gives meaning and life to all physical facts.</note> that guides them, and from which they are by their nature inseparable, far from enlightening themselves, they only sink into the most dreadful ignorance. It is solely because they have removed this Principle that **Observers** <note>original: "Observateurs"; refers to scientists who rely exclusively on sensory data and observation without considering spiritual causes.</note> search everywhere so laboriously and yet almost never agree.

It is therefore enough, I repeat, to have today uncovered for them the knot of difficulties that halts them: in the future, truth will shed its rays more abundantly, and it will reclaim, *in its own time*, the dominion that these vain sciences dispute with it today.

For my part, being too unworthy to contemplate it, I have had to limit my efforts to making it felt that it

-># Conclusion.<-

...exists, and that man, despite his wretchedness <note>original: "misere"; in the author’s mystical context, this refers to the spiritual poverty of humanity’s fallen state.</note>, could be convinced of it every day of his life, if he better governed his **will** <note>original: "volonté"; for Saint-Martin, the will is the active faculty that allows a person to reunite with the divine Principle.</note>. I would then believe myself to enjoy the most delightful reward if everyone, after having read me, said in the secret of their heart: *there is a truth, but I can turn to a higher source than men to know it.*
